blocks.heading: The Stevenson screen
blocks.text: A Stevenson screen is an instrument shelter designed to help measure representative air temperature and humidity while reducing direct effects of sunshine, precipitation and nearby heated surfaces. The familiar school model is a raised, white, louvred enclosure. Its slatted sides allow air circulation while shielding instruments. The white exterior reflects much incoming solar radiation, reducing heating of the shelter relative to a darker surface under similar conditions. A roof provides protection from direct radiation and precipitation; designs can include a double roof to reduce heat transfer. The screen is traditionally made of wood, a poor conductor of heat, so the box itself passes little of the sun’s heat to the instruments; modern shelters may use other insulating materials.

blocks.text: Thermometers need exposure to the air being measured. Direct sunshine on a sensor can heat it above the surrounding air temperature, while contact with a strongly heated wall or ground surface can introduce a different influence. The screen therefore shields the sensor without sealing it in a stagnant box. Louvre ventilation and suitable siting work together. A white sealed cupboard is not equivalent to a ventilated screen, and a louvred box against a heated wall may still produce an unrepresentative observation. Describe the design feature and then connect it to the error it helps reduce.

The screen is normally placed above a representative natural surface, often short grass, and stands on legs so that the thermometers are about 1.25 m above short grass; meteorological practice uses a standard height within roughly 1.25–2 m. Raising the instruments reduces the direct influence of surface heating while keeping the reading relevant to near-surface air. A screen on a hot paved courtyard can measure a different local environment from one over grass. That difference may be a legitimate object of study, but it should not be hidden within an attempt to compare standard observations.

blocks.text: An open site away from immediate shading and heat sources helps comparability. Buildings, trees, vehicles and reflective surfaces can affect airflow, radiation or local temperature. The aim is not to remove every influence from the atmosphere but to document exposure and reduce avoidable measurement effects. The screen should be maintained, with louvres and instruments in suitable condition. A damaged door, blocked ventilation or a sensor touching the enclosure can alter performance. Record a site change because a time series before and after moving a screen may not be directly comparable without considering the new exposure.

Door orientation should reduce direct sunlight entering while observations are taken. In the Southern Hemisphere, school siting guidance commonly uses a south-facing door; a UK north-facing instruction belongs to the opposite hemisphere and should not be copied without adjustment. The principle is shielding the instruments during reading. Open the door only as needed, avoid shading or warming the sensor unnecessarily with the observer’s body and read the appropriate scale without parallax. A thermometer removed and held in a warm hand no longer represents the same exposure as an undisturbed screen reading.

A useful supplied comparison places screen A over short grass with free airflow and screen B against a sun-heated wall with obstructed louvres. Higher readings at B could reflect the different exposure, so they should not immediately be interpreted as a regional climate difference. The comparison identifies plausible measurement influences but does not isolate which one dominates, because surface, wall proximity and ventilation all changed together. A stronger test varies one feature while controlling the others or records enough information to assess their combined effect.

Only suitable instruments belong inside the screen. Air-temperature and humidity instruments need its sheltered ventilation, while a rain gauge must collect precipitation openly and an anemometer needs appropriate wind exposure. A sunshine recorder must receive sunshine rather than be hidden in the enclosure. A station plan should therefore match each instrument to the variable and exposure it requires. Placing every instrument in one protected box would prevent several from measuring the intended element. This is a practical consequence of understanding function rather than merely recognising a labelled drawing.

These precautions connect equipment to data quality. A daily range calculated perfectly from poorly exposed thermometers can still misrepresent the intended air temperature. Consistent reading times, calibration or checks, reset procedures and clear records are needed alongside suitable siting. A local school investigation should state its exposure and limitations rather than claiming to reproduce every national observing standard. The screen reduces important unwanted influences, but it does not make all measurements from all sites identical. A supported interpretation considers both the atmospheric pattern and how the observations were obtained.
